svg.text: Example 2. A block copy into controller memory: n records from big SRAM to dst in instruction or data memory
REGISTERS.md 7.2 — one stream, mode 5 to the tile itself (d = 0): read through the address generator, back through the loopback, written by port B
DMA_CM_REMAINING = n; // n packets (2n words) to land
eject: every packet for this tile
routes each packet by its mode;
local wake: every counter done → WFI returns
modes 2, 4: at PTR[src]; mode 3: at PTR[bucket digit]; then += 2
mode 4: high 32 bits ← ordinal from DMA_RECORD_BASE_ADDRESS
SRAM read queue: one request a cycle,
a register store: the program's line
a step of the data flow (below)
The start pulse begins the run: the address generator reads STREAM[0] across the table
It makes one read request per 64-bit record, n in all, into the SRAM read queue at
The big SRAM reads the source records, in order.
Each return becomes a mode-5 packet with dst = me and addr = the cm word, which advances
The router loops it back: dst = me goes straight from injection to eject, never onto the
The traffic director routes mode 5 to port B and decrements DMA_CM_REMAINING; port B
writes the packet's two words at its packed address.
The last packet written: DMA_CM_REMAINING = 0 and cm_idle, so the local wake fires and
WFI returns. The words are in memory.
A copy into controller memory is example 1's run with mode 5: the same address generator, read queue and loopback, but the director hands the packets to
port B instead of the write engine, and each packet carries its own destination address, from the STREAM entry's cm word. Nothing on the write side chooses
addresses (REGISTERS.md 2.5). The program's code must lie outside the range it overwrites.
Source: REGISTERS.md 2.3, 2.5, 3.4, 4.3; RECIPES.md 3 (cmem_copy()); spec/machine-spec.md v1.0, §4.2, §4.11, §4.12, §6.5; the tile map is figure 1.3's.
